tagline.text: Walking an underground stream on the slopes of Mount Bandilaan in Siquijor

location.label: Location
location.text: Cantabon barangay, Siquijor town, central Siquijor Island, on the slope of Mount Bandilaan

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May dry season (dangerous in the rains)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,000 (per person, guide, entrance, gear and transport)

children.text: Cantabon Cave is a limestone cave on the slopes of Mount Bandilaan in the middle of Siquijor Island, an adventure route where you tour an underground stream, stalactites, stalagmites and small pools with a guide. You rent a helmet and flashlight, stoop, and get wet as you go in, so it suits active travelers.

Cantabon Cave is in Cantabon barangay of Siquijor town, in the middle of Siquijor Island. It sits partway up Mount Bandilaan (about 628 meters), the island's highest peak, so you ride uphill from the coastal road. In the 2024 census Siquijor town had 30,215 residents over about 90.7 square kilometers, while Cantabon barangay has only 482 residents, a quiet mountain village. From Siquijor town, riding a motorbike or tricycle up the mountain road usually takes 20–30 minutes. The island is famous for tales of witches and healers, but this cave is better enjoyed as an ordinary geological adventure. Siquijor town is old: Spanish priests arrived from about 1780, and the town and its parish were established in 1794. Average daytime highs are about
and annual rainfall is about 1,047 millimeters.

Accounts of the cave's size differ. One article puts it at about 300 meters long and up to 10 meters wide, another says about 800 meters, and one blogger cited a figure of 30 meters but could not verify it. What is certain is that the cave is pitch dark, an underground stream flows through it, and stalactites, stalagmites, terraced flowstone and clear pools follow one another. A 2007 account says foreign hunters found the cave in 1985 and that geologists at Silliman University in Dumaguete study its deposits to learn the age and type of soil in the area. This appears in only one account, so treat it as background only.

Inside, the guides have named certain spots. Reported names include the King's Bed, the Shower Bell, the Angel's Bath or Fairy's Bathtub, the Mini Pool, Mini Falls and a rock shaped like a picture frame. One account mentions a small pool near the end where you can dip your feet. Some say guides describe the water under the Shower Bell as healing and drinkable, but it is safer not to drink it for hygiene reasons. Water drips from the ceiling constantly, wetting clothes and gear, so waterproofing is essential.

Every visitor must go in with a guide. One account says a sign at the entrance states that you are not allowed to enter without a guide, and you must first register at the barangay hall. One guide takes at most three people, so a group of seven needed three guides. The entrance is narrow and may feel claustrophobic, there are sections where you stoop or crawl, and many spots are slippery. In the rainy season the water can rise and make it very dangerous, so cancel if the weather turns bad.

An underground stream runs through the cave and the passage keeps winding. You get wet and stoop as you advance, so it feels different from an ordinary tourist cave. One account says reaching the end took about 90 minutes including stops.
Large stalactites and stalagmites follow one another, along with terraced flowstone. The formations the guides have named make good photos. Keep your camera in a waterproof case.

blocks.title: The King's Bed and the Shower Bell

children.text: The best-known spots reported are the King's Bed and the Shower Bell. At the Shower Bell you can reportedly enjoy water running down from the ceiling.
There are clear pools throughout the cave, and a small cascade with a pool about 5 feet (about 1.5 meters) deep is also reported. Be ready to get wet.

blocks.title: Rules on going in with a guide

children.text: According to the entrance sign and accounts, you cannot enter without a guide. One guide takes at most three people, so book guides to match your group size and rent gear at the same time. A tip is optional, reported at about ₱100.

The start of the trail to the summit is said to be a very short motorbike ride from the cave. A reforestation center and a butterfly sanctuary are reported at the foot of the mountain. You can combine the cave and the mountain into one half-day trip.
According to one account, the cave's deposits are studied by scholars. It also works as an educational trip for learning some geology.

items.title: Half-day caving plan
items.subtitle: From the morning entry to lunch

children.text: From your lodging in Siquijor town, ride a motorbike or tricycle up the mountain road to Cantabon. The uphill ride takes about
20–30 minutes
. On the way you can stop at Guiwanon Spring Park first.

Register your visit at the barangay hall and book a guide. Rent a helmet and headlamp. One account says it was about 450 meters from the barangay hall to the cave's arch and another 143 meters on foot to the entrance.
Go in with your guide and walk inward along the underground stream and the stalactite zone. Allow about
2–3 hours
to go to the end and come back.
Come out of the cave and change out of wet clothes. Have lunch in a village at the foot of the mountain or in Siquijor town.
If you have time, climb to the summit of Mount Bandilaan. The climb, including steps, is reported at about
20 minutes
The cave is cool and wet, so your body temperature can drop. Be sure to bring a change of clothes.
Leave Siquijor town and explore Cantabon Cave.
Climb to the summit of Mount Bandilaan and look around the foot of the mountain where the butterfly sanctuary is.
Move on to Lazi for lunch.
Visit Lazi Church and Cambugahay Falls.
Fly from Manila to Dumaguete (DGT), then take a ferry from Dumaguete port to Siquijor (Larena or Siquijor port). The ferry takes about
1–1.5 hours
. Fares are reported at about
depending on the vessel class, so check the latest schedule.
Siquijor Airport is reported to have small flights from Cebu a limited number of times per week. There is reportedly no regular direct flight from Manila, so check before you book.
From Siquijor town or Larena port, ride a motorbike or tricycle uphill. The uphill ride takes about
20–30 minutes
. A 2010 article put the round trip by motorbike from Siquijor town to Cantabon at about
, but prices may well be higher now.
A motorbike rents for about
a day, and a tricycle island tour is reported at about
for three people. Decide in advance how you will get back down.

The dry season, December to May, is the safest and most pleasant. A stream runs through the cave, so when it rains heavily the water can rise and make entry dangerous. In the rainy season follow the weather forecast and your guide's judgment.

Because the plan involves going up and down a mountain road, starting early in the morning lets you finish the cave before the sun is high. The cave is not cold, but you will feel chilly coming out wet, so bring a change of clothes.

The cave is dark whatever the season, so you need lighting. Water drips from the ceiling even in the dry season, so waterproofing matters in every season. On holidays and during Holy Week, pilgrims may increase on the Mount Bandilaan side.

Cantabon village has almost no lodging, so most visitors stay in Siquijor town, Larena or on the west coast and ride up. Siquijor town is the central town with more than 30,000 residents as of 2024, so it has plenty of restaurants and small shops. Places to eat on the mountain are limited, so bring water and snacks before you set out.
One account mentions a viewpoint café in nearby Larena about 30 minutes by car from the cave, but we could not confirm whether it is open. Many places on the island need cash, so carry plenty.
Bring a waterproof case or zip bag. Water keeps dripping from the ceiling.
Wear aqua shoes or sandals. Slippers are possible, but many spots are slippery, so shoes with good traction are better.
Helmets and headlamps can be rented, but the guide's lamp may be weak, so bringing your own headlamp is safer.
One write-up says leaving trash or damaging the rock can bring a fine of up to ₱1,000 per violation.
Guides may discourage you from going deeper into the cave. Follow your guide's judgment and do not push it.
With a group, one guide goes with every three people, so budget according to your party size.
Fees and rules can change locally, so confirm the official rates at the barangay hall.

A mountain-bike tour at Mount Bandilaan is also reported, in which riders go up by truck and ride down to a village at the foot of the mountain. A guide goes along, so ask at your lodging if you are interested.
Do not enter the cave when it has rained heavily or the stream has risen. It is reported to be very dangerous in the rainy season.
The entrance is narrow and there are sections where you stoop or crawl, which can be hard for anyone with claustrophobia.
The cave is completely dark, so do not rely only on the guide's light; bring your own lighting.
The floor is slippery, so do not rush and check each step.
Sources give different lengths for the cave. Do not go beyond the section your guide has set.
Do not drink the water in the cave. Even if a guide says it is fine, you cannot verify its hygiene.

The island's highest mountain, with the uphill trail starting a very short motorbike ride from the cave. According to one account, the trail begins at a grotto with 200 steps, some steps are worn, and some of the stations of the cross have fallen. It becomes a pilgrimage site during Holy Week. The summit takes about
20 minutes
if you hurry, and at the top are three crosses and an old tower (a sign says it holds about 15 people). Another account says trees have grown up and block the view.

A three-tier waterfall in Lazi in the south of the island that can be combined with the cave into a full-day plan.
An old church in the town of Lazi in the south of the island.
